claim: MetaHiC was applied to 10 healthy human gut samples to unveil a large infection network encompassing more than 6000 interactions bridging metagenomic assembled genomes (MAGs) and phage sequences.
source: We applied a metagenomic Hi-C approach on 10 healthy human gut samples to unveil a large infection network encompassing more than 6000 interactions bridging a metagenomic assembled genomes (MAGs) and a phage sequence, allowing to study in situ phage-host ratio.
evidence: This is a direct statement of the study's main finding regarding the number of phage-host interactions detected.

claim: Three-quarters of the detected phage sequences likely correspond to dormant prophages.
source: Whereas three-quarters of these sequences likely correspond to dormant prophages, 5% exhibit a much higher coverage than their associated MAG, representing potentially actively replicating phages.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the proportion of dormant prophages based on coverage analysis.

claim: 5% of phage sequences exhibit a much higher coverage than their associated MAG, representing potentially actively replicating phages.
source: Whereas three-quarters of these sequences likely correspond to dormant prophages, 5% exhibit a much higher coverage than their associated MAG, representing potentially actively replicating phages.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the proportion of actively replicating phages based on coverage analysis.

claim: 17 sequences of members of the crAss-like phage family were detected.
source: We detected 17 sequences of members of the crAss-like phage family, whose hosts diversity remained until recently relatively elusive.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the number of crAss-like phage sequences identified.

claim: For each of the 17 crAss-like phage sequences, a unique bacterial host was identified, all belonging to different genus of Bacteroidetes.
source: For each of them, a unique bacterial host was identified, all belonging to different genus of Bacteroidetes.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the host identification for crAss-like phages.

claim: The gut virome is dominated by temperate bacteriophages belonging to the Caudovirales family.
source: The gut virome is dominated by temperate bacteriophages belonging to the Caudovirales family (Minot et al., 2011; Shkoporov et al., 2019), but how the microbiome and the virome influence each other over time remains largely unknown, with only a few studies characterizing concomitantly host-phage relationships in individual gut sample (Džunková et al., 2019; Shkoporov et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The ratio between phages and bacteria in the gut is typically assessed from the quantification of virus-like particles (VLP).
source: This ratio is typically assessed from the quantification of virus-like particles (VLP), corresponding to free phages produced during lytic cycle (Kleiner et al., 2015), with respect to the amount of bacteria cells.
evidence: This statement describes a standard methodology and is supported by a citation.

claim: First evidences indicated phage-bacteria ratios between 1 and 0.001 in the gut.
source: First evidences indicated ratios between 1 and 0.001 (Hoyles et al., 2014; Kim et al., 2011; Shkoporov et al., 2019), suggesting that the intestinal tract is quite different from other ecosystems such as oceans where phages largely outnumber bacteria (Roux et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The intestinal tract is quite different from other ecosystems such as oceans where phages largely outnumber bacteria.
source: First evidences indicated ratios between 1 and 0.001 (Hoyles et al., 2014; Kim et al., 2011; Shkoporov et al., 2019), suggesting that the intestinal tract is quite different from other ecosystems such as oceans where phages largely outnumber bacteria (Roux et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation and represents a comparative inference.

claim: Meta3C allows the assembly and scaffolding of dozens of nearly complete or complete phages and bacteria genomes, as well as their relationships, when applied on a single mammalian gut sample.
source: We notably showed that meta3C, a proximity ligation-based approach, allows the assembly and scaffolding of dozens of nearly complete or complete phages and bacteria genomes, as well as their relationships, when applied on a single mammalian gut sample (Marbouty et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: Each meta3C library was sequenced (between 43 and 206 million paired-end [PE] reads).
source: Each meta3C library was sequenced (between 43 and 206 million paired-end [PE] reads) and assembled separately using MEGAHIT (Li et al., 2015), resulting in 10 human gut assemblies ranging from 242 to 617 Mb (total size = 3.45 Gb for 1,485,156 contigs) ('Materials and methods') (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the sequencing depth achieved.

claim: 10 human gut assemblies ranging from 242 to 617 Mb were generated (total size = 3.45 Gb for 1,485,156 contigs).
source: Each meta3C library was sequenced (between 43 and 206 million paired-end [PE] reads) and assembled separately using MEGAHIT (Li et al., 2015), resulting in 10 human gut assemblies ranging from 242 to 617 Mb (total size = 3.45 Gb for 1,485,156 contigs) ('Materials and methods') (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the assembly results.

claim: 3D ratios using the standard meta3C protocol range from 1.92% to 14.58%.
source: 3D ratios using the standard meta3C protocol range from 1.92% to 14.58%, a variability that results most likely from samples heterogeneities and from the restriction enzymes used.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the measured 3D ratios.

claim: The variability in 3D ratios results most likely from samples heterogeneities and from the restriction enzymes used.
source: 3D ratios using the standard meta3C protocol range from 1.92% to 14.58%, a variability that results most likely from samples heterogeneities and from the restriction enzymes used.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the observed variability.

claim: MetaHiC protocol II applied on samples yielded an average 3D ratio of ~32% (with a min/max of 25% and 41%, respectively).
source: However, protocol II applied on samples #16016, #8015, and #9010 (using a ligation at room temperature) yields an average 3D ratio of ~32% (with a min/max of 25% and 41%, respectively).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the measured 3D ratios for the improved protocol.

claim: Protocol II yielded approximately four times more informative trans-contacts between pairs of contigs compared to meta3C, for the same cost.
source: Therefore, protocol II yielded approximately four times more informative trans-contacts between pairs of contigs compared to meta3C, for a same cost.
evidence: This is a direct comparison statement based on the measured data.

claim: Among the 1,485,156 contigs (3.45 Gb) present in the 10 assemblies, 300,677 (525 Mb) were grouped by metaTOR into 19,122 small bins ranging in size between 10 and 500 kb.
source: Among the 1,485,156 contigs (3.45 Gb) present in the 10 assemblies, 300,677 (525 Mb) were grouped by metaTOR into 19,122 small bins ranging in size between 10 and 500 kb.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the binning results.

claim: 855,633 (2.57 Gb) contigs were grouped into 1,100 larger bins containing more than 500 kb and referred to as metagenomic assembled genome (MAG).
source: An additional 855,633 (2.57 Gb) contigs were grouped into 1,100 larger bins containing more than 500 kb and further referred to as metagenomic assembled genome (MAG) (Supplementary files 4 and 5).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the MAG binning results.

claim: For each sample, the corresponding MAGs represent between 72% and 91% of all mapped reads.
source: For each sample, the corresponding MAGs represent between 72% and 91% of all mapped reads.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the proportion of reads captured by MAGs.

claim: Out of the 1,100 MAGs, 304 were identified by CheckM as 'high quality', displaying a completion rate ≥90% and contamination rate ≤5%.
source: Out of the 1,100 MAGs, 304 were identified by CheckM as 'high quality', that is, displaying a completion rate ≥90% and contamination rate ≤5%, and corresponding most likely to complete bacteria genomes, and 411 as "medium quality" (completion ≥50% and contamination ≤10%) (Figure 1c).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the quality assessment of MAGs.

claim: 411 MAGs were identified as 'medium quality' (completion ≥50% and contamination ≤10%).
source: Out of the 1,100 MAGs, 304 were identified by CheckM as 'high quality', that is, displaying a completion rate ≥90% and contamination rate ≤5%, and corresponding most likely to complete bacteria genomes, and 411 as "medium quality" (completion ≥50% and contamination ≤10%) (Figure 1c).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the quality assessment of MAGs.

claim: The phylogenetic tree covers the taxonomic groups found in a healthy human intestinal tract.
source: As expected, the trees cover the taxonomic groups found in a healthy human intestinal tract (Almeida et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation and represents an expected finding.

claim: The abundance of the different MAGs is consistent with the outcome of taxonomic analysis of the raw reads by the classifier Kaiju.
source: In addition, the abundance of the different MAGs is consistent with the outcome of taxonomic analysis of the raw reads by the classifier Kaiju (Menzel et al., 2016; Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation and reference to a figure showing the comparison.

claim: 85 MAGs (around 10%) did not present any close similarity to the GTDB-Tk references at a threshold identity of 95%.
source: Eighty-five (around 10%) of them did not present any close similarity to the GTDB-Tk references at a threshold identity of 95% (average nucleotide identity; Konstantinidis and Tiedje, 2005).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the number of novel MAGs identified.

claim: New MAGs are proportionally distributed among the different clades, with a majority belonging to Clostridia.
source: New MAGs are proportionally distributed among the different clades, with a majority belonging to Clostridia, in agreement with Pasolli et al., 2019.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation and describes the distribution of novel MAGs.

claim: VIRSorter and VIBRANT identified 4,649 and 7,918 putative phages, respectively, resulting in 9,488 unique annotated phages contigs.
source: VIRSorter and VIBRANT identified 4,649 and 7,918 putative phages, respectively (including all categories for VIRSorter and excluding identified prophages, see 'Materials and methods'), resulting in 9,488 unique annotated phages contigs, ranging in size between 1 and 10 kb.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the number of phage contigs identified.

claim: Taxonomic annotations of phage sequences confirmed the high prevalence of phages belonging to the Caudovirales order (families Siphoviridae 59%, Myoviridae 15%, Podoviridae 2%, Unassigned 22%).
source: Taxonomic annotations of those sequences using DemoVir (https://github.com/feargalr/Demovir) confirmed the high prevalence of phages belonging to the Caudovirales order (families Siphoviridae 59%, Myoviridae 15%, Podoviridae 2%, Unassigned 22%).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the taxonomic composition of identified phages.

claim: Class A corresponds to 6,503 phages contigs (out of 9,488) that can be unambiguously assigned to a single MAG based on their 3D contacts.
source: Class A corresponds to 6,503 phages contigs (out of 9,488) that can be unambiguously assigned to a single MAG based on their 3D contacts (Supplementary file 6).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the classification of phage contigs.

claim: 955 MAGs (out of 1,100) made specific contacts with one or more phage contigs.
source: In total, 955 MAGs (out of 1,100) made specific contacts with one or more of these contigs.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the number of MAGs with phage associations.

claim: The majority (6,763 out of 9,488, i.e. ~70%) of the phages present within the human gut are specific, infecting only one bacterial species.
source: These results suggest that the majority (6,763 out of 9,488, i.e. ~70%) of the phages present within the human gut are specific, infecting only one bacterial species (Figure 3a).
evidence: This is a direct statement about phage specificity based on the data.

claim: On average, a MAG was associated with 6.9 phages contigs, but this rate presented high fluctuations (SD = 7.4), with a maximum of 45 contigs.
source: On average, a MAG was associated with 6.9 phages contigs, but this rate presented high fluctuations (SD = 7.4), with a maximum of 45 contigs (MAG #9010_74_0; Supplementary file 4 and 6).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the distribution of phage associations with MAGs.

claim: Among 454 pairs of class A phages contigs belonging to the same genus but from different samples, 394 of them corresponded to phages assigned to two different MAGs presenting the same taxonomic assignment.
source: Among 454 pairs identified, 394 of them corresponded to phages assigned to two different MAGs (from the corresponding individual) but presenting the same taxonomic assignment (Figure 3—figure supplement 2a).
evidence: This statement describes a validation of the phage-host pairing strategy.

claim: 1,252 robust spacer signatures were found shared by a MAG and one or more phages sequences.
source: We found 1,252 robust spacer signatures shared by a MAG and one or more phages sequences ('Materials and methods').
evidence: This is a direct statement about CRISPR spacer matches.

claim: 387 CRISPR spacer matches were associated to a host-phage pair from the same individual.
source: Of those, 387 were associated to a host-phage pair from the same individual.
evidence: This is a direct statement about CRISPR spacer matches within individuals.

claim: Homolog phage sequences are associated to homolog MAGs sequences.
source: The plot showed that homolog phage sequences are associated to homolog MAGs sequences (Figure 3b, bottom left corner).
evidence: This statement is supported by reference to a figure showing the relationship.

claim: Very few related phages infect non-homologous MAGs.
source: In addition, while distantly related phages are occasionally found infecting homologous MAGs (Figure 3b, top left corner), very few related phages infect non-homologous MAGs (Figure 3b, bottom right corner).
evidence: This statement is supported by reference to a figure showing the relationship.

claim: Phages are 'locally adapted' to their bacterial hosts and do not easily shift from one bacterial species to another.
source: This result supports the idea that phages are 'locally adapted' to their bacterial hosts and do not easily shift from one bacterial species to another (Koskella and Meaden, 2013; Vos et al., 2009).
evidence: This statement is an interpretation supported by citations.

claim: The tree unveils clusters of closely related phages infecting the same bacterial genus (Kruskal-Wallis test, p-value=0.0132).
source: The tree unveils clusters of closely related phages infecting the same bacterial genus (Kruskal-Wallis test, p-value=0.0132) suggesting, again, that phages are specific to their hosts in human gut.
evidence: This statement is supported by statistical testing.

claim: For the 6,763 class A phages contigs, their mean read coverage ratio compared to the MAGs ratio is 1.23 (SD = 1.70), with a maximum of 58.
source: For the 6,763 class A phages contigs, their mean read coverage ratio compared to the MAGs ratio is 1.23 (SD = 1.70), with a maximum of 58.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the phage-to-host coverage ratio.

claim: The average phage-to-host coverage ratio varies from 1 (sample #10015) to 2 (sample #17006) among the 10 individual microbiota.
source: There are nonetheless significant variations among the 10 individual microbiota, as the average ratio varies from 1 (sample #10015) to 2 (sample #17006) (Figure 4—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: This is a direct statement about inter-individual variation.

claim: Phages displaying a ~1:1 ratio with their oriMAG contig (category 1, 0.5 < ratio < 2.0) represented the vast majority of the 6,239 phages-host pairs (n = 4,477; ~75%).
source: Phages displaying a ~1:1 ratio with their oriMAG contig (category 1, 0.5 < ratio < 2.0) represented the vast majority of the 6,239 phages-host pairs (n = 4,477; ~75%).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the proportion of dormant phages.

claim: Category 1 phages correspond to likely dormant (pro)phages, able to reactivate or not.
source: They correspond to likely dormant (pro)phages, able to reactivate or not.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the coverage ratio data.

claim: For 1,395 phage-hosts pairs, the corresponding oriMAG contig was significantly more covered than the associated phage (category 2 – undefined).
source: Then, for 1,395 phage-hosts pairs, the corresponding oriMAG contig was significantly more covered than the associated phage (category 2 – undefined).
evidence: This is a direct statement about a category of phage-host pairs.

claim: 367 pairs (~5%) corresponded to phages with a higher coverage than their assigned oriMAG contig.
source: The remaining 367 pairs (~5%) corresponded to phages with a higher coverage than their assigned oriMAG contig: category 3 corresponded to a ratio between 2 and 4 (n = 291) and category 4 to a ratio ≥4 (n = 76).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the proportion of potentially active phages.

claim: Category 3 and 4 phages may be or are probably actively replicating, potentially impacting the ecosystem through lytic activities.
source: These phages may be (category 3) or are probably (category 4) actively replicating, potentially impacting the ecosystem through lytic activities.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the coverage ratio data.

claim: The major part of the phages found in human gut are temperate phages with few lytic activity.
source: Overall, these results support the conclusions of former and recent work suggesting that the major part of the phages found in human gut are temperate phages with few lytic activity (Džunková et al., 2019; Minot et al., 2011; Reyes et al., 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations and the study's data.

claim: No significant correlation was detected between the presence of active phages and the abundance/growth rate of their corresponding hosts.
source: No significant correlation was detected between the presence of active phages and the abundance/growth rate of their corresponding hosts, as assessed by this analysis (Figure 4c and d).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the lack of correlation found.

claim: Bifidobacteriales and Selenomodales appear underrepresented in the targeted MAGs, which suggests that they could be less subject to phages lytic activity in the gut than other genera.
source: Bifidobacteriales and Selenomodales appear underrepresented in the targeted MAGs, which suggests that they could be less subject to phages lytic activity in the gut than other genera.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the taxonomic distribution data.

claim: 17 contigs were detected ranging in size from 58 to 176 kb and presenting several proteins homologs to the crAss-like family.
source: Using a set of representative crAss-like phages sequences (Guerin et al., 2018), we detected 17 contigs, ranging in size from 58 to 176 kb and presenting several proteins homologs to the crAss-like family ('Materials and methods').
evidence: This is a direct statement about the crAss-like phage contigs identified.

claim: The phylogenetic tree encompassing the 17 crAss-like contigs pointed at phages belonging to genera I, III, IV, VI, and V.
source: The phylogenetic tree encompassing these 17 contigs and the set of representative sequences pointed at phages belonging to genera I, III, IV, VI, and V (Figure 5 and Supplementary file 3; Low et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the phylogenetic classification.

claim: All crAss-like contigs were unambiguously assigned to MAGs belonging to the Bacteroides clade.
source: All these contigs were unambiguously assigned to MAGs belonging to the Bacteroides clade, as expected from previous predictions and co-culturing (Dutilh et al., 2014; Guerin et al., 2018; Hryckowian et al., 2020; Shkoporov et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the host assignment supported by citations.

claim: Bacteroides vulgatus, Bacteroides uniformis, Bacteroides ovatus, and Bacteroides thetaiotamicron were identified as hosts of crAss-like phages.
source: More specifically, Bacteroides vulgatus, Bacteroides uniformis, Bacteroides ovatus, and Bacteroides thetaiotamicron were identified as hosts of these crAss-like phages.
evidence: This is a direct statement about specific host identifications.

claim: Unknown species from the Prevotellaceae and Porphyromonadaceae families were detected as hosts of other crAss-like phages.
source: Interestingly, we also detected unknown species from the Prevotellaceae and Porphyromonadaceae families as hosts of other crAss-like phages.
evidence: This is a direct statement about novel host identifications.

claim: Among the 17 crAss-like contigs, nine were predicted to be circular by VirSorter.
source: Among these 17 contigs, nine were predicted to be circular by VirSorter.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the circularity prediction.

claim: 3D contacts pointed at four more circular crAss-like phage contigs.
source: 3D contacts also pointed at four more circular crAss-like phage contigs.
evidence: This is a direct statement about additional circular contigs identified.

claim: 11 crAss-like contigs exhibited a ratio ≥2 and are therefore likely multiplying.
source: Finally, the phage-host ratio of these 17 contigs showed that crAss-like phages are an active family of phages, with 11 contigs exhibiting a ratio ≥2 and therefore likely multiplying.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the activity of crAss-like phages.

claim: CrAss-like phages are an active family of phages.
source: Finally, the phage-host ratio of these 17 contigs showed that crAss-like phages are an active family of phages, with 11 contigs exhibiting a ratio ≥2 and therefore likely multiplying.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the coverage ratio data.

claim: Starting from 200 million PE reads on a single sample (#9010), the metaHiC protocol II was able to catch 81 high-quality genomes including seven from unknown species.
source: Note that, starting from 200 million PE reads on a single sample (#9010), the metaHiC protocol II was able to catch 81 high-quality genomes including seven from unknown species.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the performance of the protocol on a single sample.

claim: The relatively low number of newly recovered species suggests that the databases about the human gut microorganisms (at least those describing western population) are converging toward completion.
source: This relatively low number of newly recovered species, although still significant, suggests that the databases about the human gut microorganisms (at least those describing western population) are converging toward completion.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the novelty findings.

claim: Phages appear slightly more abundant than bacteria in the human intestinal tract but nothing comparable to other environments.
source: The phage-host ratio computed in this study suggests that phages appear slightly more abundant than bacteria in the human intestinal tract but nothing comparable to other environments (Rodriguez-Valera et al., 2009).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the phage-host ratio data supported by a citation.

claim: This work confirms that the majority of phages present in the gut are temperate phages with little or no lytic activity.
source: Therefore, this work confirms that the majority of phages present in the gut are temperate phages with little or no lytic activity (Reyes et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a conclusion supported by the study's data and a citation.

claim: Nearly 5% of the phage population exhibits a sequence coverage ratio higher than twice that of their hosts, representing actively replicating phages that could play an important role in the maintenance of the bacterial population.
source: On the other hand, nearly 5% of the phage population exhibits a sequence coverage ratio higher than twice that of their hosts, representing actively replicating phages that could play an important role in the maintenance of the bacterial population.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the proportion and potential role of active phages.

claim: Most of the phages are specific to their host and do not shift easily to another host, at least in the human intestinal tract.
source: The work also confirms that most of the phages are specific to their host and do not shift easily to another host, at least in the human intestinal tract (Koskella and Meaden, 2013; Vos et al., 2009).
evidence: This is a conclusion supported by the study's data and citations.

claim: Meta3C/HiC unveiled the host, at the species level, of 17 crAss-like contigs, all belonging to different members of the Bacteroides clade.
source: In a single analysis, meta3C/HiC unveiled the host, at the species level, of 17 crAss-like contigs, all belonging to different members of the Bacteroides clade.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the host identification results.

claim: This result is in agreement with previous prediction at the class level.
source: This result is in agreement with previous prediction at the class level (Dutilh et al., 2014), and suggests crAss-like phages are widely distributed in the Bacteroides clade.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation and represents agreement with prior work.

claim: CrAss-like phages are widely distributed in the Bacteroides clade.
source: This result is in agreement with previous prediction at the class level (Dutilh et al., 2014), and suggests crAss-like phages are widely distributed in the Bacteroides clade.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the host identification results.

claim: CrAss-like phages share features characteristics to both phages and plasmids and generally encode proteins allowing for their own replication.
source: CrAss-like phages share features characteristics to both phages and plasmids and generally encode proteins allowing for their own replication.
evidence: This is a statement about the characteristics of crAss-like phages.

claim: The crAss-like phages are reminiscent of the concept of plasmid or phage plasmid.
source: The crAss-like phages are therefore reminiscent of the concept of plasmid or phage plasmid (Lagos and Goldstein, 1987).
evidence: This is an interpretation supported by a citation.
